summary: The video blends a philosophy of creating depth and motion in landscape imagery with a practical, step-by-step Photoshop workflow. The speaker explains a zone-based approach to processing complex scenes, distinguishing one-, two-, and three-zone shots, and emphasizes how different parts of a frame (sky, foreground, background) often require distinct adjustments. The transcript then drills into hands-on techniques: cropping decisions, RAW adjustments (brightness, whites, color temperature, and calibration), and painting adjustments with the History Brush to selectively apply light, color, and texture. Recurrent motifs include building directional light, forming near-to-far transitions, and using diffusion, luminosity, and glow to create painterly depth. The video also contrasts the relative simplicity of drone (one-zone) shots with multi-zone scenes, and it closes with practical notes on versioning, cloning versus painting, and the value of preserving a workflow that supports iterative refinements.

sections.title: Intro: depth, motion, and viewer engagement
sections.description: The speaker frames the goal of landscape processing as creating depth and a sense of motion within a single frame. He emphasizes transitions (near to far, cool to warm, dark to light) and identifies the blacks as the most important transition. He classifies shots as two-zone and implies more zones increase processing difficulty.

sections.title: Zone System in practice: two-, three-, and one-zone shots
sections.description: The narrator explains how foreground, sky, and background may each require separate processing paths (zones). He notes that multi-zone scenes cannot usually be kept in RAW adjustments alone because edits for the sky can negate edits for the cactus/foreground. Drone shots are described as single-zone and comparatively easier to process.

sections.title: Defining focal points and guiding eye through light and form
concepts: strongest light as a focal cue
near-to-far transitions as fallback in the absence of a single focal point
sections.description: The speaker outlines how to steer the viewer’s eye by establishing a focal point via light, and he discusses the role of triangular forms and layered elements to direct attention. He covers what happens when a single focal point isn’t obvious, recommending a near-to-far progression to maintain visual flow.

sections.title: Initial RAW/Photoshop workflow and crop decisions
concepts: two-step RAW adjustments: darker base, whites up, warmth
introducing color balance via blues and calibration
sections.description: The presenter discusses crop choices early in the workflow and demonstrates basic RAW adjustments (darken, raise whites, warm highlights) followed by a color-grade pass using blues and camera calibration. He also emphasizes cropping to remove distractions and framing considerations for directional light.

sections.title: History Brush and forward/back history workflow
concepts: painting adjustments from the future state
hard edge vs soft brush for precision
refining masks and transitions with undo/redo
sections.description: A core technique shown is painting adjustments from a chosen history state using the History Brush. The workflow includes selecting a future state, applying light or color to targeted regions with hard or soft brushes, and then smoothing with erasers and soft brushes to maintain natural transitions. The speaker stresses the flexibility of moving between steps and re-editing non-linearly.

sections.title: Global diffusion, luminosity, and painterly glow
concepts: Orton glow as a stylistic choice
color grading refinements and saturation control
sections.description: The video covers applying diffusion and luminosity to create a painterly look, including a cautionary note about the Orton glow being a subjective effect. The speaker demonstrates iterative RAW adjustments and selective painting to balance warm and cool tones, followed by La-based tweaks to ensure color consistency.

sections.title: Drone-shot depth: practical depth separation and zone-specific edits
concepts: two-zone drone shots: foreground vs background
diffusion and light balancing in the background
local adjustments for horizon, river, and peaks
sections.description: Examples include two-zone drone shots where the foreground and background require different adjustments. The speaker discusses creating depth through selective diffusion and color balance, noting how background contrast and diffusion help distinguish layers in aerial compositions.

sections.title: Wrap-up: workflow philosophy, versioning, and quick-footed processing tips
concepts: overall rule: depth, motion, and transitions are constant goals
sections.description: The closing section reinforces the speaker’s overarching philosophy: all images seek depth and motion through deliberate transitions. He discusses practical habits such as saving multiple versions for safety, comparing clone-paint to history-based methods, and keeping a workflow that preserves speed while allowing iterative refinements. He also references additional videos and resources for deeper philosophy and technique.

featured_techniques.technique: Zone System: two-, three-, and one-zone processing for landscape scenes
History Brush: painting forward RAW adjustments onto targeted regions
Crop-first workflow: deciding crop/warp early in Photoshop
Global diffusion and luminosity to create painterly depth (Orton glow as option)
D-Haze and color grading: balancing color with advanced RAW/Camera Raw controls
Clone Paint workflow: borrowing light and texture between frames, compared to history-based edits
Dodge tool cautions: avoiding color shifts; selective light shaping via painting instead
